title.value: Scalar Invariant Networks with Zero Bias
title.justification: The title directly mentions the key focus of the paper, which is scalar invariant networks and the zero bias concept in neural networks.
title.quote: Scalar Invariant Networks with Zero Bias Chuqin Geng Xiaojie Xu

extractions.description: This paper explores the concept of scalar invariance in neural networks, specifically focusing on image classification tasks. It argues for the removal of bias terms, showing through empirical results that zero-bias neural networks possess scalar invariance, allowing them to maintain prediction accuracy even with varying contrast in images. The study extends this property to different neural network architectures, including CNNs and ResNets, and highlights potential robustness benefits from this approach.

sustainable_development_is_central.justification: The main focus of the paper is on a technical innovation in machine learning related to neural networks' performance in image classification, specifically regarding bias terms and scalar invariance. There is no direct mention or significant focus on ecological impact or climate sustainability.
sustainable_development_is_central.quote: Just like weights, bias terms are learnable parameters in many popular machine learning models, including neural networks. Biases are believed to enhance the representational power of neural networks, enabling them to tackle various tasks in computer vision.

primary_category.justification: The paper focuses on technical improvements in neural network architecture for image classification tasks, which do not have direct implications or applications in Climate or Ecological Sustainable Development.
primary_category.quote: We believe dropping bias terms can be considered as a geometric prior when designing neural network architecture for image classification, which shares the spirit of adapting convolutions as the translational invariance prior.

secondary_categories.quote: Our empirical results suggest that zero-bias neural networks can perform comparably to normal networks for practical image classification tasks.
